segments.text: Probability provides the mathematical foundation for statistical inference — every hypothesis test and confidence interval in later chapters rests on the probability concepts developed here.

is any subset of the sample space (a specific outcome or combination of outcomes of interest). Correctly and completely defining the sample space is often the most important step in solving a probability problem, since a miscounted or incomplete sample space invalidates every subsequent calculation.

Probability assigns a number between 0 and 1 to every event, following three basic axioms: every probability is non-negative, the probability of the entire sample space is 1 (something must happen), and for mutually exclusive events, the probability of their union is the sum of their individual probabilities. Every other probability rule can be derived from these three axioms.

This is especially useful in diagnostic and classification problems (for example, finding the probability a patient has a disease given a positive test result, when what is actually known from clinical data is the probability of a positive test given the disease is present or absent) and frequently produces results that are counter-intuitive without careful calculation, particularly when the underlying event is rare.

(expected value) of a random variable is its probability-weighted average — the long-run average value it would take over many repetitions, which need not itself be a value the variable can actually take on any single trial (e.g., the expected value of a fair die roll is 3.5, though no single roll ever gives 3.5).

items.text: Correctly defining the sample space is the essential first step; probability rules follow from three basic axioms (non-negativity, total probability 1, additivity for mutually exclusive events).
The addition rule subtracts overlap to avoid double-counting; the multiplication rule requires conditional probability unless independence holds.
Independence (knowing one event doesn’t change the other’s probability) is distinct from — and effectively opposite to — mutual exclusivity, which implies strong dependence.
Bayes’ theorem reverses a known conditional probability to find the reverse conditional probability, essential for diagnostic and classification reasoning.
A random variable’s expectation is its probability-weighted long-run average, not necessarily an achievable single-trial value.
